authoredPrompt: This figure shows a labeled cross-sectional diagram of a Downs cell, the industrial electrolytic apparatus used to produce pure sodium metal from molten sodium chloride via the reaction 2NaCl(l) → 2Na(l) + Cl2(g). The cell interior contains a bath of molten NaCl, with a cylindrical iron screen separating the electrode compartments; the cathode (−) occupies the outer annular region and the anode (+) projects upward from the bottom center, both connected to an external voltage source at the lower right. Liquid sodium metal, which is less dense than the molten salt, rises and collects in a side reservoir on the right, from which it drains through a labeled Na outlet; simultaneously, Cl2 gas produced at the anode rises through a central green-tinted collector tube and exits through a labeled Cl2 outlet at the upper right, while fresh NaCl is fed continuously through an inlet at the top. The iron screen physically segregates the two products — liquid sodium and gaseous chlorine — preventing their recombination and enabling continuous, separate collection of each. This figure demonstrates the Downs cell as the industrial-scale process for sodium production and explains why aqueous electrolysis cannot substitute for it, since H+ ions are more easily reduced than Na+ ions at any cathode in contact with water.
authoredInteractions:
- Animate the electrolysis: show Cl- ions migrating toward the central anode and Na+ ions moving to the outer cathode, with Cl2 gas rising through the outlet and liquid sodium collecting at the Na outlet
- Click each electrode region: highlight the half-reaction occurring there and display the balanced half-equation
authoredContext:
The most important method for the production of sodium is the electrolysis of molten sodium chloride; the set-up is a Downs cell , shown in . The reaction involved in this process is:

Separation of the molten sodium and chlorine prevents recombination. The liquid sodium, which is less dense than molten sodium chloride, floats to the surface and flows into a collector. The gaseous chlorine goes to storage tanks. Chlorine is also a valuable product.

Pure sodium metal is isolated by electrolysis of molten sodium chloride using a Downs cell. It is not possible to isolate sodium by electrolysis of aqueous solutions of sodium salts because hydrogen ions are more easily reduced than are sodium ions; as a result, hydrogen gas forms at the cathode instead of the desired sodium metal. The high temperature required to melt NaCl means that liquid sodium metal forms.

A diagram is shown. At the center of the diagram is a T-shaped structure labeled, “Anode ( positive sign ),” that is on a mesh-like background labeled, “Iron screen.” The anode is connected to a box labeled, “Voltage source,” by a line, and the voltage source is connected to one of two L-shaped structures that surround the anode. They are labeled, “Cathode ( negative sign ).” Above the cathode on the right side of the diagram is a tube connected to a collection chamber labeled, “N a metal,” that has a lower outlet labeled, “N a outlet.” Surrounding all of these components is a blue background labeled, “Molten N a C l,” and a series of tubes that form a square outside the diagram. They have an opening in the upper right corner labeled, “Inlet for N a C l.” At the top of the diagram is a large tube with an upward-facing arrow drawn on it. The tube turns right, has a right-facing arrow on it, and is labeled, “C l subscript 2 outlet.”

discrepancies: Several intended two-line labels render as concatenated text without spacing or line breaks, such as 'MoltenNaCl', 'Ironscreen', 'Inlet forNaCl', 'LiquidNa metal', and 'Voltagesource', unlike the clean separated labels in the source.

The default figure adds many labeled moving Na⁺/Cl⁻ ions and product bubbles; the source only shows small unlabeled pale speckles in the molten salt region, so the default state is more cluttered than the static textbook figure.
The sodium collection vessel and outlet on the right are simplified and proportioned differently from the source, with a narrower pipe-like reservoir and less faithful vertical bulb/neck shape.
The voltage source is smaller, shifted, and its internal label is cramped compared with the larger, clearly labeled gray box in the source.
Some leader lines and labels are too close to the artwork or overlap visually, especially around the left-side molten NaCl/iron screen labels and the right-side sodium labels.
The external wiring and lower support/flange details are present but simplified and not as faithful to the source geometry.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure is clearly recognizable as a Downs cell and the electrolysis interactions are conceptually useful, but malformed multiline labels and extra default ion animations reduce its fidelity as a static textbook replacement.
action_items: Fix the multiline SVG text helper so tspans have explicit x and dy offsets, preventing labels like 'MoltenNaCl' and 'Voltage source' from collapsing into unreadable concatenated strings.
Make the default state closer to the source by hiding labeled moving ions until animation is enabled, or replace them with small unlabeled pale speckles matching the original.
Refine the right-side liquid sodium collector and outlet geometry to better match the source vessel proportions and bends.
Resize and reposition the voltage source and its label so the text is legible and the wiring more closely follows the original.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction structure are strong, but the main problems are implementation-level issues with SVG multiline labels, default clutter, geometry proportions, and voltage-source layout.
